questions.question: What is the main purpose of this warning at the beginning of the passage?
questions.answer: It prepares readers by explaining why the book may be hard to understand and why people can still benefit from it.

questions.question: What example is used to show that different readers may gain different amounts from the book?
questions.answer: The passage compares the book to a garden where each person can reach only some of the fruit, but still gets enough benefit.

questions.question: What does that garden example teach about readers with different abilities?
questions.answer: It teaches that the work is not only for one type of reader, and people with greater understanding may take more from it.

questions.question: How many reasons are given for why the book is difficult?
questions.answer: Five reasons are given.

questions.question: What is the first reason for the difficulty of the book?
questions.answer: The writer says he recorded his own findings in his own way for himself, not by adjusting them to how other people usually understand things.

questions.question: How does the second reason connect to the subject of Allah’s oneness?
questions.answer: The book discusses belief in Allah’s oneness in a very wide and deep way, so many people cannot grasp it all at once.

questions.question: Why might one sentence become very long in this book?
questions.answer: A sentence may become long so a large truth is kept whole instead of being broken apart.

questions.question: According to the third reason, why does one proof sometimes need so much before it?
questions.answer: It needs a lot of preparation first so the proof can be understood properly.

questions.question: What is the fourth reason the discussion sometimes feels lengthy?
questions.answer: Many topics have lots of proofs and evidences, so the writer includes many demonstrations.

questions.question: According to the passage, who may struggle with that many proofs?
questions.answer: People with limited understanding may find it hard to follow.

questions.question: What personal conditions affected the writing of the treatise in the fifth reason?
questions.answer: The writer was upset, physically sick, and wrote quickly.

questions.question: Why did the writer not go back and revise the first draft?
questions.answer: He felt he was not writing purely from his own choice, so he thought it was not suitable to rearrange or correct it by his own later thoughts.

questions.question: Besides haste and illness, what other things added to the difficulty of the book?
questions.answer: Some parts were in Arabic, and one section written completely in Arabic was taken out and made into a separate work.

questions.question: What overall message does the passage give to a reader before starting the book?
questions.answer: Even if the book is challenging, every sincere reader can still receive some benefit from it.

questions.question: What does the passage say about whether every reader will fully understand the whole treatise?
questions.answer: It says not everyone will understand all of it.

questions.question: What hopeful point is given right after that?
questions.answer: No one will be left without some share of benefit.

questions.question: Why is the image of fruit in a garden a good comparison for this treatise?
questions.answer: It shows that people can take what they are able to reach, even if they cannot take everything.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the purpose of the “garden”?
questions.answer: It is meant for many people, not just one person.

questions.question: What does the first cause tell us about the style of the book?
questions.answer: Its style comes from the writer’s own understanding rather than being shaped for other people’s habits of thinking.

questions.question: In the second cause, what makes the topics especially hard to understand?
questions.answer: They are very broad, very deep, and sometimes very long.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about understanding deep topics quickly?
questions.answer: It suggests that such topics cannot always be understood all at once.

questions.question: In the third cause, why does the writer avoid splitting up a large truth too much?
questions.answer: He wants to protect the full meaning of the truth instead of weakening it by breaking it apart.

questions.question: What can we infer about the book’s sentences from the third cause?
questions.answer: Some sentences may be unusually long because they carry a lot of connected meaning.

questions.question: How does the fourth cause differ from the third cause?
questions.answer: The third is about the size of each truth and the need for preparation, while the fourth is about having many proofs for the same matter.

questions.question: What does the fifth cause show about the writer’s condition while writing?
questions.answer: He was going through hardship and sickness and wrote in a rushed state.

questions.question: How did Ramadan relate to the writing of the treatise?
questions.answer: The spiritual inspiration for it came during Ramadan.

questions.question: Why did the writer think editing the text later might be wrong?
questions.answer: He felt the writing did not come simply from his own personal will, so changing it by his own later ideas seemed unsuitable.

questions.question: What final detail in the fifth cause may make the book harder for some readers?
questions.answer: Parts of it are in Arabic, and one fully Arabic section was separated from the rest.

questions.question: What two ideas are balanced in the opening lines of the passage?
questions.answer: The passage balances difficulty in full understanding with the promise that everyone can still gain something.

questions.question: How does the passage encourage a reader who feels weaker than others in understanding?
questions.answer: It says even if someone cannot reach everything, the share he can reach is still enough for him.

questions.question: What can be learned from the comparison between shorter and longer reach in the garden example?
questions.answer: Readers have different abilities, and that difference is expected and accepted.

questions.question: What is introduced after the opening comparison?
questions.answer: Five causes are listed to explain why the book is hard to understand.

questions.question: In the first cause, what is one major difference between this book and many other books?
questions.answer: This one was written from the writer’s own direct understanding instead of being arranged around other people’s viewpoints.

questions.question: How does the second cause describe the treatment of Divine unity in the book?
questions.answer: It presents that belief in a very complete and far-reaching way.

questions.question: Why would such a treatment make the book challenging for some readers?
questions.answer: Because the topics become very wide and deep, which can be hard to take in quickly.

questions.question: According to the third cause, what happens when one truth is very large?
questions.answer: Explaining it may require a sentence that runs very long.

questions.question: Why are long introductions or lead-ins sometimes needed before a proof?
questions.answer: They help set up the proof so the truth is not misunderstood or cut apart.

questions.question: What does the fourth cause say about the number of proofs used?
questions.answer: Some matters are supported by many proofs and evidences, sometimes as many as ten or twenty.

questions.question: How might that many proofs affect a reader?
questions.answer: It can make the discussion feel wordy and difficult to follow.

questions.question: What circumstances in the fifth cause kept the writer from polishing the draft?
questions.answer: He was distressed, ill, writing quickly, and believed the writing came in a way that should not be altered by later personal editing.

questions.question: What language issue is mentioned in the fifth cause?
questions.answer: Some Arabic passages remained in the work.

questions.question: What happened to the first main section that was fully in Arabic?
questions.answer: It was removed from this work and turned into a separate piece.

questions.question: What does the passage say a reader should not expect before reading this treatise?
questions.answer: A reader should not expect that everyone will fully understand every part of it.

questions.question: What should a reader still expect, even if the book is difficult?
questions.answer: A reader should expect to receive at least some benefit.

questions.question: What does the garden picture help the reader understand about fairness?
questions.answer: It shows the book can still be fair and useful even if different people take different amounts from it.

questions.question: Why is the image of people with longer reach important in the comparison?
questions.answer: It reminds readers that some people are able to grasp more, and the work is also meant for them.

questions.question: What is the first listed reason for the book’s difficulty?
questions.answer: It was written from the writer’s own personal observations and understanding.

questions.question: How might writing “for himself” make the book harder for others?
questions.answer: It may not match the usual ways other readers expect ideas to be explained.

questions.question: What special feature of the subject matter is named in the second reason?
questions.answer: The subject is belief in Allah’s oneness presented in a very comprehensive way.

questions.question: Which qualities of the topics are named in the second reason?
questions.answer: They are described as very broad, very deep, and sometimes very long.

questions.question: In the third reason, what is the danger the writer wants to avoid?
questions.answer: He wants to avoid breaking up a large truth into pieces.

questions.question: Why may one proof include many earlier points before reaching the proof itself?
questions.answer: Because the proof needs a lot of groundwork first.

questions.question: What is the main complaint someone might have because of the fourth reason?
questions.answer: Someone might feel the discussion goes on too long because so many proofs are included.

questions.question: What does the passage say about some readers’ ability to handle that style?
questions.answer: It says some people with limited understanding cannot handle it well.

questions.question: What physical and emotional struggles are mentioned in the fifth reason?
questions.answer: The writer mentions distress and several illnesses.

questions.question: What three writing-related results came from the fifth reason?
questions.answer: The book was written quickly, not revised, and left with some Arabic parts, including one section moved into a separate work.

questions.question: At the start of the passage, how are readers reassured even before the difficulties are listed?
questions.answer: They are reassured that every reader can receive some portion of benefit.

questions.question: What lesson about learning can be taken from the garden example?
questions.answer: A student does not need to master everything at once in order to benefit.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the amount a person can gain from the book?
questions.answer: Each person gains according to what he is able to reach.

questions.question: What does the writer do after giving the garden example?
questions.answer: He explains five reasons that the book may be hard to understand.

questions.question: What writing approach in the first reason may make this treatise different from more common books?
questions.answer: The ideas are expressed from the writer’s own way of seeing them, not adjusted to other people’s understandings.

questions.question: Why does the second reason make the book sound demanding for readers?
questions.answer: The book deals with very large and deep matters connected to Allah’s unity.

questions.question: What does the phrase about not understanding everything “all at once” suggest?
questions.answer: It suggests readers may need time and patience to understand the book.

questions.question: In the third reason, why might a single sentence cover so much?
questions.answer: Because one sentence may carry a whole major truth without splitting it apart.

questions.question: What does the third reason say about the structure of a proof?
questions.answer: A proof may need many introductory parts before the main point is complete.

questions.question: How does the fourth reason add another layer of difficulty beyond long sentences?
questions.answer: It says that many different proofs may be given for one matter, making the explanation even longer.

questions.question: What does the passage mean by saying limited minds may not understand this?
questions.answer: Some readers may struggle to follow a discussion that is so full of detail and repeated evidence.

questions.question: In the fifth reason, what spiritual source is mentioned for the treatise?
questions.answer: Its lights or inspirations are said to have come from Ramadan.

questions.question: Why is the writer’s lack of revision important for understanding the style of the book?
questions.answer: It helps explain why the wording may feel rough, difficult, or less organized.

questions.question: What final information about language and structure appears at the end of the passage?
questions.answer: It says some Arabic sections remained, and the first section, which was entirely in Arabic, was separated into its own work.

questions.question: What overall attitude toward the reader appears in the opening of the passage?
questions.answer: It is honest about the book’s difficulty but encouraging about the benefit readers can still receive.

questions.question: How does the opening comparison help a student who feels discouraged?
questions.answer: It teaches that not reaching everything does not mean failure, because even a smaller share can still be valuable.

questions.question: What does the comparison suggest about the book itself?
questions.answer: It is rich in meaning, like a place filled with many things to benefit from.

questions.question: After the comparison, what organizing pattern does the passage use?
questions.answer: It lists five separate causes of difficulty one by one.

questions.question: In the first cause, what is one reason the book may not feel easy or familiar to readers?
questions.answer: It was not written to fit the normal understanding of other people.

questions.question: In the second cause, what makes the subject matter weighty and hard?
questions.answer: It discusses the truth of Allah’s unity in a very complete and far-reaching manner.

questions.question: What three descriptions are used for the topics in the second cause?
questions.answer: They are wide in scope, deep in meaning, and sometimes long in explanation.

questions.question: In the third cause, why is keeping a truth unbroken important?
questions.answer: Because dividing a major truth too much could weaken or damage how it is understood.

questions.question: What can we infer about the reading pace needed for this book from the third cause?
questions.answer: Readers may need to slow down and follow long explanations carefully.

questions.question: What is the reason for the extra length mentioned in the fourth cause?
questions.answer: The writer often gives many supporting proofs and evidences for the same matter.

questions.question: How is the problem in the fourth cause different from simple repetition?
questions.answer: The added length comes from demonstration and support, not from meaningless repeating.

questions.question: What difficulties in the writer’s life are mentioned in the fifth cause?
questions.answer: He was troubled, sick, and writing in a hurried condition.

questions.question: What belief about the writing process made the writer avoid changing the draft?
questions.answer: He felt the writing did not come merely from his own personal choice, so altering it later seemed improper.

questions.question: According to the fifth cause, what two textual features may challenge readers at the end?
questions.answer: The presence of Arabic passages and the removal of the fully Arabic first section into a separate work.
